summary: This RFC suggests a simple way for workstations to dynamically access mail from a mailbox server. It revises RFC 918 and is Post Office Protocol version 2. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Your mail waits in a box, and your computer can come and check it. This is the second edition of the rules for that.

questions: what is the difference between acks and ackd
subtitle: An early, deliberately simple protocol for fetching mail from a mailbox server to a workstation.

tldr.problem: Workstations are often powered down and cannot act as mail servers, so a user's mailbox should live on an always-up server. The workstation needs a simple way to read that mail.
tldr.mechanism: POP2 is a short command and reply protocol over a reliable stream such as TCP, on port 109. The client logs in with HELO, reads a message with READ and RETR, and then acknowledges it with ACKS, ACKD or NACK.
tldr.outcome: RFC 937 is Historic. It revised RFC 918 and the server keeps no state from one session to the next.

today: RFC 937 has Historic status. It obsoleted RFC 918, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What POP2 Is For
sections.content:
The Post Office Protocol Version 2 (POP2) lets a user's workstation access mail from a mailbox server. Mail is expected to be posted from the workstation to the server by SMTP, described in RFC 821 and RFC 822.

POP2 assumes a reliable data stream such as TCP or any similar protocol. When TCP is used, the POP2 server listens on port 109. The memo is a revision of RFC 918 and is presented as a proposed protocol for the ARPA-Internet community.
sections.plainLanguage: POP2 is the set of rules for a computer to collect its mail from a mailbox kept somewhere else.

sections.title: System Model and Philosophy
sections.content:
The workstation is an Internet host, but it is not expected to hold the user's mailbox. The mailbox belongs on an always up server, while a workstation may often be powered down and unavailable as an SMTP server. So mail for John Smith is addressed to JSmith@DOG-HOUSE.ARPA, the server, and not to his machine FIDO. The user is not tied to any one workstation.

POP2 is designed for workstations and servers on low-delay, high-throughput local networks such as Ethernets. In a substantially different environment, a different division of labor and a different protocol may be appropriate.

The protocol is very simple and is not a user interface. One basic rule is "if anything goes wrong close the connection", and another is to have few options. POP2 does not parse messages or analyze headers such as Date:, From:, To:, Cc: or Subject:. It just transmits whole messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Your mail lives at a mailbox that is always open, like a post office box, instead of on your own computer, which might be switched off. The rules are kept very short, and if anything goes wrong the call simply ends.

sections.title: Commands and the Reading Cycle
sections.content:
The server listens for a connection and sends a greeting. The client waits for it and sends HELO with a user name and password. The server answers with the number of messages in the default mailbox. The client may use FOLD to select another mailbox, which also returns a message count.

READ begins a message reading transaction and may name a message number. The default is the current message, which is incremented when a message is read and set to one when a new folder is selected. The server replies with the number of characters in the message, and RETR then asks for the message data.

After the data the client must send one acknowledgment. ACKS means the message was received and should be kept. ACKD means it was received and should be deleted. NACK means it was not received and should be kept. With ACKS or ACKD the current message indicator moves on, and with NACK it stays. Each reply gives the length of the now current message. The client ends with QUIT.

Deletion is lazy: ACKD only marks a message. The change is made when the mailbox is released at the end of the session or when FOLD selects another mailbox, and messages are not renumbered until then.
sections.plainLanguage: You log in, ask how many letters there are, ask for the next one, and read it. Then you tell the post office to keep it, throw it away, or send it again because it got lost on the way.

sections.title: Conventions and Reply Formats
sections.content:
Commands and replies end with a carriage return and line feed (CRLF). Message length is a character count of the whole transmitted message, with CRLF counting as two characters. A length of zero means the message does not exist or is empty, and asking to transmit a zero-length message makes the server close the connection. Messages are sent in the Internet format of RFC 822 in NVT-ASCII. All numbers are decimal and message numbers start at one.

A backslash is the quote character in command arguments, so a space in a password is sent as backslash and space. It is not used in the mail data sent after RETR.

Every reply begins with one required character: a plus sign for success, a minus sign for failure, an equals sign for a length and a number sign for a count of messages. The text after it is up to the implementer. The greeting is a plus sign, then POP2, then the server host name. The RFC also lists default mailboxes: MAIL.TXT.1 in the login directory on TOPS-20, and /usr/spool/mail/user or files under /usr/user/Mail/inbox/ on UNIX.
sections.plainLanguage: Every answer starts with a little sign: a plus for yes, a minus for no, an equals for how long a letter is, and a hash for how many letters there are.

sections.title: Client and Server States
sections.content:
The RFC gives state diagrams and decision tables for both sides. The client moves through the states CALL, NMBR, SIZE, XFER and EXIT. The server moves through LSTN, AUTH, MBOX, ITEM, NEXT and DONE.

Anything unexpected is treated as garbage. On the client the action is to send QUIT and go to EXIT. On the server it is to send an error reply and close the connection. If an unauthorized user sends HELO, the server also sends an error and closes the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer and the server each follow a little map of what is allowed next. Step off the map and the call ends.

sections.title: Timeouts, Sizes and Limits
sections.content:
The client expects a reply quickly, with a short timeout called T1, but it must allow for servers that need time to count messages or reformat a message, and must not time out during a long RETR transfer. The server uses a longer timeout T2 while waiting for the next command. T2 can be small for clients that send commands without waiting for a person, and must be large when a person decides between commands.

A command line is at most 512 characters, including the command word and CRLF. A reply line is at most 512 characters, and a text line at most 1000 characters. The RFC says ISI built a POP2 server for TOPS-20 and Berkeley 4.2 Unix, and clients for an IBM-PC and Berkeley 4.2 Unix.

The server does not examine message headers and keeps no state between sessions, so it cannot send only the new messages. The RFC has no security section; the only access control it describes is the user name and password carried by HELO.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides wait only so long for an answer, so nobody gets stuck. Lines also have a size limit, so nothing gets too big to handle.

items.label: Hello
items.desc: Identifies and authenticates the user; the reply is a message count.

items.label: Folder
items.desc: Selects another mailbox or folder; the reply is a message count.

items.label: Read
items.desc: Begins a message reading transaction; the reply is the message length.

items.label: Acknowledge and Save
items.desc: Received; keep the message in the mailbox.

items.label: Acknowledge and Delete
items.desc: Received; mark the message for deletion.

items.label: Negative Acknowledge
items.desc: Not received; keep the message and stay on it.

items.label: Quit
items.desc: Ends the session; the server replies + OK and closes.

items.label: Length
items.desc: Number of characters in a message.

items.label: Count
items.desc: Number of messages in a mailbox.
